documents.title: Joint Commission National Patient Safety Goals NPSG medication safety

chunks.content: WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN ON THIS TOPIC Medication reconciliation reduces medication prescription errors and improves patient safety. The utilisation of health informatics tools plays a critical role in facilitating effective medication reconciliation. WHAT THIS STUDY ADDS This study highlights the need for quality improvement teams using information technology to understand the clinical context and human elements at play. Applying critical thinking, technology advancements and human factor principles significantly improved department of medicine outpatient medication reconciliation compliance rate from an average of 80% in August 2023 to 97% in April through September 2024. This improvement was maintained. HOW THIS STUDY MIGHT AFFECT RESEARCH, PRACTICE OR POLICY While technology yields promising results, overcoming barriers, such as lack of time, insufficient access to complete medication information or communication gaps between providers and patients, is key to improving medication reconciliation processes and achieving better patient outcomes. Addressing these challenges necessitates understanding of both technological advancements and human factor principles as well as robust interdisciplinary collaboration and training. The department of medicine’s outpatient medication reconciliation improvement initiatives can be replicated in other departments and healthcare organisations. Problem The department of medicine outpatient medication reconciliation compliance objective was increased to 92% in accordance with SSMC senior leadership’s desire to enhance patient safety and move towards safer practices; nevertheless, meeting this higher goal proved difficult. According to an analysis of the first two quarters of 2023 performance data, the department of medicine’s average outpatient medication reconciliation compliance rate was persistently below the new goal of 92%, at 80%. Background Medication reconciliation involves the systematic review of a patient’s medication regimen during transitions in healthcare to prevent medication errors like omissions, duplications, dosing errors and drug interactions that can significantly impact patient safety. It involves verifying the medications a patient is currently taking, comparing them with the patient’s prescriptions and resolving any discrepancies. The Joint Commission has underscored the importance of medication reconciliation as a National Patient Safety Goal due to its impact on mitigating medication errors and enhancing patient safety. A significant proportion of adverse drug events arises from unrecognised medication discrepancies during transitions of care, highlighting the necessity for robust medication reconciliation protocols. This is consistent with findings in various healthcare settings, wherein structured medication reconciliation processes have been shown to significantly reduce medication-related errors and improve clinical outcomes. The utilisation of health informatics and electronic medical record (EMR) systems plays a critical role in facilitating effective medication reconciliation in the outpatient setting. While technology yields promising results, overcoming barriers, such as lack of time, insufficient access to complete medication information or communication gaps between providers and patients, is key to improving medication reconciliation processes and achieving better patient outcomes. Addressing these challenges necessitates understanding of both technological advancements and human factor principles as well as robust interdisciplinary collaboration and training. The use of technology to refine electronic medication lists and provide reminders for patients underscores the critical intersection of human factors and technology in improving medication reconciliation compliance rates. The role of education, both for healthcare providers and patients, cannot be understated. Adequate education and training for healthcare professionals are necessary to ensure that they understand their roles in medication reconciliation and are equipped to use relevant technologies effectively. Active patient participation in their own care is vital for effective medication reconciliation and significantly contributes to improved outcomes. Patients should be encouraged to bring their medications to appointments and familiarise themselves with their medication regimens. This concept of patient engagement is necessary to ensure continuity of care and minimise medication errors. Human factor engineering plays a crucial role in enhancing medication safety and effectiveness in outpatient settings. Research shows that focusing on human factors can foster better teamwork and communication among healthcare providers, which is integral during patient care transitions where the potential for errors is significantly increased. The integration of human factor principles in system designs can help anticipate user needs and improve the overall usability of technology in clinical settings, further supporting the argument that a systematic approach to medication reconciliation can significantly mitigate the risk of medication errors during patient transitions. Baseline measurement According to an analysis of the first two quarters of 2023 performance data, the department of medicine’s average outpatient medication reconciliation compliance rate was persistently below the new goal of 92%, at 80%. Design The outpatient medication reconciliation procedures in the internal medicine, cardiology, pulmonology, gastroenterology, rheumatology, nephrology, neurology, haematology, oncology and infectious disease clinics of the SSMC department of medicine were examined using a prospective study methodology. Information was gathered from 133 328 patient visits over the 14-month trial period, which ran from August 2023 to September 2024. The pharmacy informatics team audits using the EMR systems, which are essential for monitoring medication reconciliation compliance metrics, made it easier to retrieve information. medication reconciliation compliance rate was persistently below the new goal of 92%, at 80%. Design The outpatient medication reconciliation procedures in the internal medicine, cardiology, pulmonology, gastroenterology, rheumatology, nephrology, neurology, haematology, oncology and infectious disease clinics of the SSMC department of medicine were examined using a prospective study methodology. Information was gathered from 133 328 patient visits over the 14-month trial period, which ran from August 2023 to September 2024. The pharmacy informatics team audits using the EMR systems, which are essential for monitoring medication reconciliation compliance metrics, made it easier to retrieve information. Before the quality improvement methods were put into place, the average department of medicine outpatient medication reconciliation compliance rate was 80%. Strategy Outpatient medication reconciliation improvement efforts were initiated across all department of medicine outpatient specialty clinics including internal medicine, cardiology, gastroenterology, pulmonology, nephrology, neurology, rheumatology, infectious disease, haematology and oncology clinics. Our aim was to improve the department of medicine outpatient medication reconciliation compliance rate to meet the new target of 92% by 14 months. To accomplish this goal, a multidisciplinary department of medicine Outpatient Medication Reconciliation Improvement Taskforce was formed and led this quality improvement project. The team included members from physicians, quality, pharmacy, pharmacy informatics and the department of information technology. We used usability testing to evaluate how easy and effective it is for the physicians to use the outpatient medication reconciliation tool. Taskforce members went to the clinics and observed in real time the department of medicine outpatient physicians completing the outpatient medication reconciliation. This helped us understand through direct real-time feedback the usability issues and challenges of using the medication reconciliation tool and how to improve the tool design for better user experience. Physicians stated that the main challenge in using the medication reconciliation tool is the fact that there were multiple active duplicates of the same medication and that patients do not bring their home medications to the clinic visit. Physicians explained that the medication reconciliation tool has a forcing function that will not allow them to sign the medication reconciliation until all active medications are reviewed and either continued, discontinued or new medications prescribed, and with the many duplicates of the same medication, this was time-consuming and challenging especially in a busy clinic with limited clinic time for each patient. When patients were asked why they did not bring their home medications to the clinic visit, they responded that they either forgot or did not know they needed to bring their medications. Brainstorming sessions were conducted, and we used a fishbone diagram to identify root causes for outpatient physician medication reconciliation tool non-compliance as well as coming up with ideas and solutions to address those areas for improvement. By engaging in critical thinking and utilising technology and human factors, the team implemented several interventions targeting the root causes of outpatient medication reconciliation non-compliance. Among these interventions, enhancing the EMR system and using human factor principles to engage both healthcare providers and patients were key. The interventions were tested through a series of Plan, Do, Study and Act (PDSA) cycles and their impact on improving the outpatient medication reconciliation compliance was monitored. The strategic interventions implemented included engaging patients actively in the medication reconciliation process, optimising the EMR system for clearer medication lists and conducting refresher training sessions for physicians. These initiatives were designed to overcome barriers such as inefficiencies and lack of comprehensive medication lists, making it easy for both healthcare providers and patients to do the right thing and minimise workarounds. PDSA cycle Plan The department of medicine outpatient specialty clinic providers faced challenges with medication reconciliation due to incomplete medication histories and inefficiencies in the medication reconciliation process. The multidisciplinary taskforce team identified three key areas for intervention: improving patient awareness, optimising the EMR system and providing refresher training for physicians. The goal was to enhance the accuracy and efficiency of the outpatient medication reconciliation process and achieve the hospital’s set compliance target of 92%. Do In the implementation phase, various interventions were rolled out from October 2023 onwards. Initially, efforts were directed at improving patient awareness. A reminder to bring home medications was incorporated into automated text messages sent to patients prior to their clinic appointments. Additionally, a message that emphasised the importance of bringing home medications to the clinic visit was displayed on all overhead monitors in the department of medicine outpatient specialty clinics ( ). Following this in November 2023, an EMR cleanup initiative was undertaken, removing duplicate medication entries older than 1 year, which burdened the medication reconciliation process. This optimisation facilitated a more concise and accurate medication list that helped healthcare providers complete the medication reconciliation process more efficiently. Subsequently, a web-based physician refresher training was conducted in December 2023 aimed at improving the healthcare providers' use of the medication reconciliation electronic

Additionally, a message that emphasised the importance of bringing home medications to the clinic visit was displayed on all overhead monitors in the department of medicine outpatient specialty clinics ( ). Following this in November 2023, an EMR cleanup initiative was undertaken, removing duplicate medication entries older than 1 year, which burdened the medication reconciliation process. This optimisation facilitated a more concise and accurate medication list that helped healthcare providers complete the medication reconciliation process more efficiently. Subsequently, a web-based physician refresher training was conducted in December 2023 aimed at improving the healthcare providers' use of the medication reconciliation electronic tool. All physicians receive formal training on medication reconciliation as part of the onboarding process. Mandatory targeted department of medicine web-based physician refresher training with presurveys and postsurveys was conducted with 100% completion rate. The training focused on common challenges, efficient workflows and best practices for accurate outpatient medication reconciliation. Study Over the 14-month study period, from August 2023 to September 2024, data were compiled from 133 328 patient visits. The extraction of information was facilitated by the pharmacy informatics team audits utilising the EMR systems, which play a key role in tracking medication reconciliation compliance metrics. Act Successful interventions derived from the implementation phase were fully integrated into routine clinic operations. Enhanced patient reminders were established as standard operating procedures throughout all outpatient clinics. Additionally, a quarterly EMR review process was initiated to mitigate the reaccumulation of unnecessary duplicate entries. Ongoing web-based medication reconciliation training modules were integrated into annual education programmes for physicians to maintain competency and adherence to medication reconciliation best practices. It became evident that the interventions implemented not only led to an immediate rise in outpatient medication reconciliation compliance rates but also established a promising framework for sustained improvement moving forward. The ability to replicate these successful strategies across other departments became inherent to the broader goals of patient safety and improved outcomes across the organisation. Results Data from the EMR audits revealed a significant improvement in the department of medicine outpatient medication reconciliation compliance rates, rising from 80% in August 2023 to successfully meeting the new target of 92% by January 2024 and further achieving 97% compliance rate in April through September 2024 ( ). Lessons and limitations SSMC senior leadership support and empowerment was one of the key success factors for this quality improvement project. However, fostering buy-in and engagement from healthcare providers posed challenges due to a perceived belief that the medication reconciliation electronic tool was challenging to use and time-consuming, especially in a busy clinic environment. Addressing these misconceptions through targeted physician refresher training helped overcome resistance and improve compliance. However, continuing to sustain these improvements will require ongoing leadership support and meaningful engagement with healthcare providers at all levels. There is a lot of evidence to support that improving medication reconciliation reduces medication errors. The limitation of this study is that the reduction in prescription medication discrepancies associated with the improvement in medication reconciliation compliance was not studied to assess the impact of improving medication reconciliation on patient safety. Conclusion The department of medicine was able to not only reach but surpass the new outpatient medication reconciliation objective through a team effort and several effective interventions that drew on technology and human factor principles. The department of medicine’s outpatient medication reconciliation compliance rate increased from an average of 80% in August 2023 to 97% in April through September 2024 as a result of the performance improvement measures that were put into place. This study highlights the need for quality improvement teams using information technology to understand the clinical context and human elements at play. For an outpatient medication reconciliation procedure to be effective, technology and human factor concepts must be integrated. Effectively involving patients and healthcare professionals in the outpatient medication reconciliation process facilitates the shift to more effective and long-lasting medication reconciliation systems and helps overcome opposition. Healthcare professionals can promote a safer transition of care, reduce prescription errors and improve the general standard of patient care by utilising technology in conjunction with human factors concepts. The department of medicine’s outpatient medication reconciliation improvement initiative paved the way for possible replication in other departments and healthcare organisations by disseminating the lessons acquired from this quality improvement project throughout the hospital.

chunks.content: 1 Problem The implementation of improvements in the surgical routine to increase compliance to the 19-item checklist - World Health Organization Surgical Safety Checklist (WHO SSC) - remains a challenge: there is no consensus regarding best practices and there are no guidelines available in the literature for this purpose. However, there is agreement concerning the need for intensive training of teams and engagement of staff as an essential measure for the appropriation of WHO SSC by professionals for use in clinical practice. Hospital Moinhos de Vento (HMV), located in the city of Porto Alegre, southern Brazil, is a large 497-bed institution performing an average of 2,000 surgeries monthly. In the past decades, many strategies to improve internal processes have been implemented at HMV, which in 2002 was the first hospital in the South of Brazil to be accredited by the Joint Commission International. In this context, five years ago HMV adopted the WHO SSC. For each surgical procedure, an electronic WHO SSC form must be completed by the nursing team. Adherence to completion of the electronic form, including all checklist items, reached 100%. However, after some time, it became evident that even though the electronic form was filled, not all WHO SSC phases were correctly or routinely performed. Therefore, the risk management team, in partnership with Surgery Center medical and nursing leaders, performed on-site checks over a two-month period. The results showed use of the WHO SSC in 87% of surgeries in the first month and 79% of the surgeries in the second month – that is, on average, 400 procedures every month were performed without application of this safety enhancement mechanism. In this context, the aim was to increase the use of the WHO SSC to 100% of performed surgeries compared to current practice. 2 Background Health care-related adverse events (AE) are frequent, and approximately 40% occur in operating rooms (OR). Nevertheless, 50% of these events are preventable [ ]. To reduce this type of preventable injury, in 2008 the World Health Organization (WHO) proposed the WHO SSC. This tool aims at improving compliance with procedures to be performed preoperatively to minimize the risk of intraoperative AE and postoperative complications. The WHO SSC involves specific steps to be followed in three phases: 1) before anesthesia induction (Sign In); 2) before surgical incision (Time Out); 3) and before the patient leaves the OR (Sign Out) [ ]. In the past decade, many studies have confirmed the effectiveness of the WHO SSC to reduce morbidity and mortality, perioperative complications, and length of stay [ , , ]. This evidence has contributed to the prompt adoption of this tool by many institutions worldwide. However, the challenges of implementing the WHO SSC, considered to be a complex social intervention [ ], have been pointed out and discussed in many studies, including some that question the usefulness of the WHO SSC [ , ]. The difficulties linked to WHO SSC implementation are often associated with institutional scenarios in which the checklist was introduced without adequate supporting strategies. Factors such as top-down implementation of the WHO SSC, lack of intensive team training, and mandatory implementation demanded/imposed by regulatory agencies have all been associated with failure, with no improvement in patient outcomes [ , ]. Many investigations have shown that professionals often do not use the WHO SSC correctly, or simply complete the WHO SSC at the end of the surgical procedure, rather than preoperatively [ , , , ]. Also, despite the existence of a manual and other materials to support WHO SSC implementation, this process is not standardized, and in general formal training of teams is not performed [ , ]. In Brazil, studies have shown that the WHO SSC is used inconsistently, with limited compliance, especially when it comes to the Time Out phase [ , ]. Therefore, the present study examines the role of patient safety infrastructure, organizational leadership involvement, and education and training as necessary aspects for effective implementation of the WHO SSC. As noted, the mere introduction of the WHO SSC as a task, without adequate staff or leadership training, may lead to loss of interest and in some cases to disregard of the tool by the surgical team. At HMV, electronic records showed 100% compliance with the WHO SSC. However, close monitoring at the Surgery Center revealed that teams did not comply with some WHO SSC items, or in some cases ignored the WHO SSC. 3 Baseline measurement Data were initially collected from the HMV information system. In addition, compliance data were obtained through on-site monitoring by the risk management team in July and August 2015 ( ). 4 Design The HMV strategic goals include the continuous improvement of internal processes as to ensure that all activities performed at the hospital are safe. Therefore, actions aimed at improving quality

HMV, electronic records showed 100% compliance with the WHO SSC. However, close monitoring at the Surgery Center revealed that teams did not comply with some WHO SSC items, or in some cases ignored the WHO SSC. 3 Baseline measurement Data were initially collected from the HMV information system. In addition, compliance data were obtained through on-site monitoring by the risk management team in July and August 2015 ( ). 4 Design The HMV strategic goals include the continuous improvement of internal processes as to ensure that all activities performed at the hospital are safe. Therefore, actions aimed at improving quality and patient safety are strongly supported and encouraged. In this scenario, the present quality improvement strategy was implemented with the strategic support of the leadership. The planning and execution of activities involved the risk management team, surgeons and nurses, Surgery Center leaders and decision-makers, and Surgery Center teams. 4.1 Intervention The present intervention aimed at engaging surgeons and raising the awareness of teams regarding the need to use the WHO SSC. For that, the WHO SSC was presented as an evidence-based tool with proven effectiveness. That involved discussions about patient risk and real-world safety issues experienced by surgeons. Also, training and education activities were performed, with empowerment of the surgical nursing team to use and, most importantly, to initiate the WHO SSC. 4.2 The intervention encompassed a) Adaptation of WHO SSC structure and content to the local context. b) Involvement of medical leadership: during the intervention period, the chief Surgery Center surgeon discussed WHO SSC data with physicians from all specialties during routine monthly meetings. The emphasis was on the need for continuous improvement. He also taught a structured evidence-based class showing the effectiveness of the WHO SSC and its very low (virtually zero) cost. As an awareness-raising strategy, he then proposed a comparison between the high cost/limited benefit of developing antineoplastic drugs [ ] vs. low cost/recorded impact as high as 30% in improvement of surgical outcomes associated with WHO SSC implementation [ ]. c) Sharing of scientific evidence by head surgeons in each specialty: head surgeons acted as multipliers within their specialty teams. They supported the chief surgeon in presenting WHO SSC use indicators at the monthly scientific meetings held by each specialty. They also encouraged open discussions on patient safety during surgery, and mediated experience exchanges and reports of situations involving safety failures, with or without consequences for the patient. c) Education, training, and empowerment of Surgery Center nursing teams through on-site meetings with risk management staff; standardization of structural and practical aspects relating to the use of the WHO SSC as part of the work flow; encouragement for nursing teams to proactively initiate the WHO SSC Time Out phase immediately before the start of the procedure, directing the pertinent questions to surgeons and anesthetists whenever these physicians did not initiate the WHO SSC themselves; empowerment of nursing team to avoid conflict; nursing team guidance regarding how to report disruptive attitudes and behaviors; resolution of disruptive attitude and behavior cases through face-to-face meetings with chief Surgery Center surgeon. 5 Strategy The aim was to increase the use of the WHO SSC to 100% of performed surgeries compared to current practice. A Plan, Do, Study, Act (PDSA) cycle was implemented. Following implementation of the intervention strategy, as described in Design, WHO SSC compliance was locally audited by a risk management team member. Daily monitoring was performed during 26 months. The intervention was initially assessed considering the rate of WHO SSC compliance. However, because the aim was to promote learning and continuous improvement, with adjustments in the way the WHO SSC was used, after 12 months the assessment criterion was changed to emphasize to the most critical phase – Time Out. Time Out entails a pause: all activities must stop and team members must focus on the review of relevant details of the procedure that is about to begin. The first month of on-site observation using this assessment criterion revealed 21% compliance, in August 2016 ( ). The improvement intervention was repeated throughout September. To increase Time Out compliance, the chief Surgery Center surgeon called new meetings (repetition of intervention) with specialty teams, focusing on scientific evidence supporting use of the WHO SSC . The Surgery Center nursing team and the institution's risk manager organized education and training activities for nursing teams focusing on a detailed examination of the Time Out phase. The requirement of pausing to perform the Time Out step was the main approach. The results show immediate response, with increasing Time Out compliance, as shown in . Data were continuously collected over 14 months for assessment of the effectiveness and sustainability of the intervention. 6 Results Baseline data showed 100% completion of the WHO SSC electronic form. However, on-site checks revealed compliance of 87% in June

of the WHO SSC . The Surgery Center nursing team and the institution's risk manager organized education and training activities for nursing teams focusing on a detailed examination of the Time Out phase. The requirement of pausing to perform the Time Out step was the main approach. The results show immediate response, with increasing Time Out compliance, as shown in . Data were continuously collected over 14 months for assessment of the effectiveness and sustainability of the intervention. 6 Results Baseline data showed 100% completion of the WHO SSC electronic form. However, on-site checks revealed compliance of 87% in June 2015 and 79% in July 2015. Following the first intervention, in August 2015, increasing compliance was detected, with a steadily ascending curve during the entire period. Mean WHO SSC usage after the intervention was 89%. As described in the Strategy section, all monitoring checks were performed on-site daily during 26 months ( ). In August 2016, the intervention analysis criterion was changed, and the monitoring of Time Out was initiated. The baseline check revealed 26% conformity with the Time Out pause prior to the start of the procedure. After the intervention was repeated, in September 2016, data monitoring revealed an ascending compliance curve. The percent conformity varied from 60% to 90%, showing increased Time Out compliance ( ). 7 Lessons and limitations The objective of the quality improvement strategy was to achieve 100% WHO SSC compliance compared to current practice. The results do not allow us to infer a direct causal effect of the intervention on WHO SSC use. However, it is possible that the process of engaging and training the Surgery Center team, with involvement of decision-makers, did provide an important contribution to increase WHO SSC adherence, even though the initial goal of 100% was not met. Continuous data monitoring, during 26 months, showed a lasting increase in compliance, indicating that the strategy has some degree of sustainability. The success of the quality improvement strategy might be related to the engagement of the entire Surgery Center team (physicians, nurses, and nursing technicians), to the ensuing empowerment of the nursing team, and to the intense participation of the risk management team and of physicians and nursing in leadership roles (decision-makers). This is in accordance with the literature, which shows from frontline feedback and engagement of leaders is essential to develop, implement, and increase adherence to interventions aimed at promoting safety [ , , ]. In addition, the strategy of showing scientific evidence that support the use of WHO SSC was also effective to raise awareness among physicians. These results corroborate previous findings showing skepticism among surgeons and anesthetists regarding the available evidence. Interestingly, it has been reported that some believe the available evidence to be inconclusive, and thus they do not support broad implementation of the 10.13039/100004423 WHO SSC [ ]. A key moment that translated into learning for the entire team was the decision to change the intervention analysis criterion. The objectives consisted in promoting learning, continuous improvement, and improving the manner the WHO SSC was used. Thus, monitoring compliance with the most critical WHO SSC phase, Time Out, was initiated. This assessment showed that, despite the intervention and the continuous learning taking place, compliance with Time Out never reached 100% for all items. This is an important datum that reveals the complexity involved in the expected pause during which safety items are checked right before the start of the procedure. According to the literature, further research is necessary to shed light on the means and tools that will ensure that system-level interventions such as the WHO SSC are effectively integrated into practice rather than being seen as just one among many resources [ , , ]. In addition, all data during the analysis and monitoring indicate that the strategy employed, which did not entail direct implementation cost, is promising to increase the effective use of the WHO SSC. It should also be noted that the present results cannot be generalized given the great influence of local context and institutional culture on paradigmatic issues relating to patient safety and the WHO SSC. Also, the main limitation of the present strategy must be mentioned – which is the fact that only one on-site verification of the Time Out was performed prior to the start of the second intervention round, which focused on improving Time Out compliance. Nevertheless, repeating, monitoring, and adjusting the analysis criterion was important because, despite increased and sustained WHO SSC compliance in the first 12 months of intervention, it became clear that the most critical step, Time Out, was often skipped. Therefore, sharing our experience may contribute to the development of future interventions or WHO SSC-related research. Strong points of the quality improvement strategy include the use an explicit method, namely the Institute for Healthcare Improvement's Plan-Do-Study-Act

only one on-site verification of the Time Out was performed prior to the start of the second intervention round, which focused on improving Time Out compliance. Nevertheless, repeating, monitoring, and adjusting the analysis criterion was important because, despite increased and sustained WHO SSC compliance in the first 12 months of intervention, it became clear that the most critical step, Time Out, was often skipped. Therefore, sharing our experience may contribute to the development of future interventions or WHO SSC-related research. Strong points of the quality improvement strategy include the use an explicit method, namely the Institute for Healthcare Improvement's Plan-Do-Study-Act model [ ], which facilitated the understanding of the intervention/improvement process and allowed the exploration of the method's full potential. In addition, the change in criterion of analysis was duly documented, as recommended by existing international guidelines [ ] on the design, performance, and reporting of improvement projects, which require flexibility especially in the design and implementation phases [ ]. 8 Conclusion It is the first article of this kind in Brazil. The data show that adjustment of WHO SSC structure and content to the local context, as well as engagement of decision-makers and risk management staff to promote WHO SSC compliance contributed to the success of the proposed intervention. The engagement of surgeons in evidence-based discussions and the education, training, and empowerment of the nursing team represent a promising quality improvement strategy, which was sustainable and increased real-world WHO SSC compliance. Finally, the present learning and continuous improvement experience may be useful to the global surgical community, which must strive to ensure that the WHO SSC is not an end in itself – a checklist that must be filled and followed to fulfill a task – but rather a part of the care process associated with successful surgical procedures. chunks.content: TAHUN [MANUJU: MALAHAYATI NURSING JOURNAL, ISSN CETAK: 2655-2728 2023 ISSN ONLINE: 2655-4712, VOLUME 5 NOMOR 2 FEBRUARI 2023] HAL 461-468 GAMBARAN PENGELOLAAN OBAT LASA (LOOK- ALIKE SOUND-ALIKE) DI APOTEK GOGE FARMA Fariz Miftahurrozik1*, Nova Adi Firmansah2, Sari Prabandari3 1-3 Politeknik Harapan Bersama Tegal Email Korespondensi: sayiman15@gmail.com Disubmit: 29 September 2022 Diterima: 03 November 2022 Diterbitkan: 01 Februari 2023 DOI: https://doi.org/10.33024/mnj.v5i2.7966 ABSTRACT The arrangement of drug storage should pay attention to LASA drugs which can sometimes cause medication errors due to errors in taking from the drug storage rack. It is necessary to develop a drug management system to overcome these medication errors. Identification of LASA drugs, high-alert drug use policies, and safe prescription writing policies also contribute significantly to reducing the incidence of medication errors. The main objective of drug management is the availability of drugs of good quality, available in types and quantities that are in accordance with the needs of pharmaceutical services for people in need. The type of research used is descriptive non-experimental research using a qualitative approach, carried out in July 2022 at the Goge Farma Pharmacy Tegal. The number of samples used in this study was 5 informants consisting of the Pharmacist in Charge of the Pharmacy (APA) and the Pharmaceutical Technical Personnel (TTK) who worked at the Goge Farma Pharmacy. The results of this study indicate that 100% of Goge Farma Pharmacies have carried out LASA Drug Management in accordance with Standard Operating Procedures (SOP) properly. The data obtained from this research is by distributing several questionnaire sheets to the Pharmacist in Charge of the Pharmacy (APA) and Pharmaceutical Technical Personnel (TTK) and conducting open interviews with Pharmacists in Charge of the Pharmacy (APA). Keywords: Management, Arrangement, Storage, LASA ABSTRAK Penataan penyimpanan obat hendaknya memperhatikan obat LASA yang terkadang dapat menimbulkan medication error akibat kesalahan pengambilan dari rak penyimpanan obat. Perlu dikembangkan sistem manajemen penataan obat untuk mengatasi medication error tersebut. Identifikasi obat-obat LASA, kebijakan penggunaan obat high alert dan kebijakan penulisan resep yang aman juga memberikan kontribusi signifikan terhadap pengurangan insiden kesalahan medication error. Tujuan utama pengelolaan obat adalah tersedianya obat dengan mutu yang baik, tersedia dalam jenis dan jumlah yang sesuai kebutuhan pelayanan kefarmasian bagi masyarakat yang membutuhkan. Jenis Penelitian Yang digunakan adalah penelitian non ekperimental yang bersifat deskriptif dengan menggunakan pendekatan kualitatif, dilaksanakan pada bulan Juli 2022 di Apotek Goge Farma Tegal. Jumlah sampel yang digunakan dalam penelitian ini sebanyak 5 informan yang terdiri dari Apoteker penanggung Jawab Apotek 461 TAHUN [MANUJU: MALAHAYATI NURSING JOURNAL, ISSN CETAK: 2655-2728 2023 ISSN ONLINE: 2655-4712, VOLUME 5 NOMOR 2 FEBRUARI 2023] HAL 461-468 (APA) dan Tenaga Teknis Kefarmasian (TTK) yang bekerja di Apotek Goge Farma.
